name: Emeka Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Emeka. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me the public version and what you really think. Can you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new connections crew on the east side of the city, where they're throwing up housing estates as fast as they can. So most days we're setting poles or pulling cable for a new street, putting in the transformer, and hooking up houses one by one. Lately it's a lot of solar panels and car chargers too, people wanting bigger supplies. I like it because you can see the street grow.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pace and the money. The developers want everything yesterday, and we're short a person most weeks. I came in on the newer contract, so I'm paid less than the guys who've been there fifteen years for the same job. Priya and I are getting married next summer, and between the rent and the wedding fund there's maybe three weeks of money in the bank at any time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I asked one to help with the wedding budget, which was depressing. At work I've used it once or twice to look up a regulation when the code book wasn't in the van. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped, but it's handy for small stuff. I'd probably joke at work that the chatbot still can't dig a trench. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes nothing for me really. The houses still need connecting. My job's safe as long as they keep building, and it seems like they always will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep my head down, keep putting money in the wedding fund. Maybe push for the newer contract guys to get levelled up with the old contract, because that's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just another normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the gap between the old and new contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About ten percent, plus the old guys get a better pension. Over a year that's most of a honeymoon. I'm doing the same job as Ray next to me, and he's getting a honeymoon I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the union rep and the supervisor, like a normal person. I'm not going to make a big scene. If they don't move, I'll keep asking every year until they do.

S0.say: Fair enough, it was overhyped, but it's handy for small things. He'd joke that the chatbot still can't dig a trench.
S0.think: It changes nothing for him, because new houses still need connecting and the building never seems to stop.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving for the wedding. Raises the gap between old and new contracts with the union rep and supervisor, calmly and every year.
S0.quote: I'm doing the same job as Ray next to me, and he's getting a honeymoon I'm not.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka's measured approach to the pay gap shows his pragmatic, middle-of-the-road style. His job is tied to housing growth, which gives him a sense of safety. The wedding is the backdrop to every money decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, it happens, and the smart thing is to learn what you need. I'd say that to the younger lads on the crew. Online, nothing, I'm not on there much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my bit of the job might actually grow. More solar, more batteries, more car chargers, all need bigger connections. Maybe the planning and paperwork gets automated, which honestly I'd like. The risk is they use machines to need fewer of us on the trenching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first guys to try any new tools, then ask them how it went and get on the training. I'd keep saving for the wedding. And I'd use the AI stuff a bit more at work for the regulations, since everyone else would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you watch first, to see if a new tool works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, the guy on the old contract. He hates new stuff, so if Ray says it's all right, it's all right. If Ray says it's not rubbish, that's better than any sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you change your plans for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this one. People still have jobs, the estates still get built. We'd go ahead, maybe a bit smaller just to be careful.

S1.say: Change happens and the smart thing is to learn what you need. He'd tell the younger crew members that, but wouldn't post about it.
S1.think: His part of the job may grow with solar, batteries and car chargers, and he'd welcome automated paperwork. The risk is fewer people needed on trenching.
S1.do: Waits for colleagues to test new tools, then asks them and joins the training. Keeps saving for the wedding and uses AI a bit more for regulations at work.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a little curious.
S1.quote: If Ray says it's not rubbish, that's better than any sales pitch.
S1.fieldNote: He uses his most sceptical colleague as a test for new kit, which is a classic steady approach. He sees the shift to solar and car chargers as more work for his crew. The wedding goes ahead in this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast and the government needs to catch up, with some kind of support for people who lose work. But I'd also say people need to get practical, not just panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Three weeks of money, a wedding booked, and a job that suddenly might not exist. If robots can build estates, they can connect them. And the estates might stop anyway if nobody has a job to pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd move the wedding to something small at Priya's parents' garden and get the deposit back on the hall if we could, that's about two thousand. Then I'd cut everything else and put that money aside. I'd watch which jobs the robots aren't doing yet and try to get into one fast, maybe the robot installation crews themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A sinking feeling in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Priya go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset about the hall, she's had her heart set on it. But she's practical, she'd say people matter more than the venue. We'd end up married in her mum's garden with a borrowed sound system, and honestly we'd probably be fine with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robot installation crews? How sure are you that they'd hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. I'd be one of hundreds trying for the same thing. I'd have to wait and see who gets in first, and then push hard.

S2.say: It's happening too fast and the government needs to catch up with support for people who lose work. People also need to get practical, not just panic.
S2.think: It scares him: three weeks of money, a booked wedding and a job that may vanish. If nobody has work, the estates might stop being built anyway.
S2.do: Moves the wedding to Priya's parents' garden and tries to recover about two thousand from the hall deposit. Cuts spending, saves the difference and tries to get onto robot installation crews.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a sinking feeling in his stomach.
S2.quote: We'd end up married in her mum's garden with a borrowed sound system, and honestly we'd probably be fine with it.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline goes straight to the wedding, the one thing he and Priya have planned. He notes the knock-on effect that estates might stop if nobody can pay a mortgage. He is honest that his plan to join robot crews is a long shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people time to prepare if they're sensible. I'd tell the guys on the crew to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to pick up a second trade, but only just. My best bet is something that'll be needed during the switch, like battery and solar installation, because that'll boom for a while before the robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my domestic electrician's licence at night school, which takes about eighteen months. That lets me do home solar and batteries on weekends for extra cash. I'd still have the wedding, but smaller, and we'd save the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for night school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about a thousand for the course. I'd ask the company if they'd pay part, since it's related, and if not I'd spread it over a year. It's a thousand for the course, or about the same as the flowers Priya wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm scrambling. Five years, I can actually finish a course and get a few years of use out of it. That's the main thing.

S3.say: Five years gives sensible people time to prepare. He'd tell his crew to start thinking about it now.
S3.think: Five years is just enough for a second trade. Battery and solar installation should boom during the switch, before robots catch up.
S3.do: Starts an eighteen-month night course for a domestic electrician's licence, at about a thousand, asking the company to share the cost. Plans a smaller wedding and does home solar work on weekends for extra money.
S3.feel: Anxious but not frozen, because he'd be doing something.
S3.quote: It's a thousand for the course, or about the same as the flowers Priya wanted.
S3.fieldNote: He chooses a bridge trade that would boom during the transition, which is a practical, timing-based plan. He weighs the course cost against wedding flowers. He doesn't expect it to last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be caught out. I'd say it to the crew and to Priya's brothers, who all think it'll never happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven, probably with a kid by then. I think I could ride the connections work for a while, get the electrician's licence, and then see what's left. I'm not that worried, honestly, as long as I don't waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrician course in the first couple of years, but at a normal pace. Keep the wedding as planned, maybe a bit smaller. Start putting a fixed amount aside every month, even fifty, so there's something by the time it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a kid by then. Would this change when you have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd have them a bit earlier, actually, while I've definitely got work. Better to have the baby while I've still got a job than to wait and find out I haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a decision you'd talk through with Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. She'd probably want to wait for her nursing promotion first. We'd work it out together, that's how we do everything.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be caught out. He'd say it to his crew and to Priya's brothers, who think it'll never happen.
S4.think: He'd be 37, probably with a child. He could ride the connections work, get an electrician's licence and see what's left, and isn't very worried if he uses the time well.
S4.do: Does the electrician course at a normal pace over the first couple of years and keeps the wedding roughly as planned. Puts a fixed amount, even fifty a month, aside every month.
S4.quote: Better to have the baby while I've still got a job than to wait and find out I haven't.
S4.fieldNote: The surprise was that a long timeline might make him want children sooner, while his job is certain. He frames every big decision as a joint one with Priya. His calm depends on not wasting the decade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It hits right when we're getting married and have nothing saved. What would help is the company paying for retraining while you're still working, so you don't have to quit to learn something. And maybe some temporary support from the government, but connected to finding new work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about what happens to the new estates. Everyone talks about the jobs. If nobody has a job, who's buying the houses I'm connecting? That's what I'd want someone to answer.

headlineQuote: If nobody has a job, who's buying the houses I'm connecting?
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old lineworker on a new-connections crew in a fast-growing suburb, wiring up housing estates, solar panels and car chargers. He's on a newer, lower-paid contract and is saving for a wedding with his fiancée Priya, with about three weeks of money in the bank. He's practical, uses AI now and then, and waits for sceptical colleagues to test new tools before he jumps in. He's calm through AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, expecting his work to grow, but AGI by 2028 alarms him and would shrink the wedding to a garden. Given five or ten years, he'd add a domestic electrician's licence and might have children sooner while his job is secure.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as he's getting married with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid retraining while still working, and some temporary government support connected to finding new work.
